theme: Jonathan’s faith; Saul’s foolishness; Saul rejected
readingInstruction: Read 1 Samuel 14:1-15:35. Chapter 14 shows Jonathan’s faith and Saul’s rash vow. Chapter 15 records Saul’s final rejection. Pay close attention to Samuel’s words in 15:22-23.
settingTheScene: Israel is still under Philistine pressure. Jonathan, Saul’s son, takes the initiative against a Philistine outpost, trusting that the LORD can save by many or by few. Later, God commands Saul through Samuel to destroy the Amalekites, who had attacked Israel in the wilderness. Saul’s partial obedience is the failure that ends his dynasty. These chapters mark the turning of the kingdom from Saul toward David.
observation: Jonathan says to his armor-bearer, “It may be that the LORD will work for us, for nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few” (14:6).
Saul makes a rash oath that no one may eat before evening, and Jonathan, who did not hear it, eats honey (14:24-27).
The people ransom Jonathan, and he is not put to death (14:45).
The LORD tells Saul to strike Amalek and devote all that they have to destruction (15:1-3).
Saul spares King Agag and the best of the sheep and oxen (15:9).
Saul says, “I have performed the commandment of the LORD,” and Samuel answers, “What then is this bleating of the sheep in my ears?” (15:13-14).
“To obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams” (15:22).
“The LORD has rejected you from being king over Israel” (15:26). And “the Glory of Israel will not lie or have regret” (15:29).
interpretation:
Jonathan is a bright figure in a dark story. He and his armor-bearer climb a cliff against a garrison, and his words show a faith that does not depend on numbers: “Nothing can hinder the LORD from saving by many or by few.” The LORD gives a great victory. Jonathan’s faith contrasts with his father’s, who stays under a pomegranate tree and then binds the army with a foolish oath. Saul’s religion is concerned with rules and ceremony, but his heart does not trust God. The oath nearly costs Jonathan his life.

Chapter 15 is the decisive moment. The command against Amalek is a hard one, part of the judgment on a people whose long violence had been judged by God. Saul obeys in part. He spares the king and the best animals, and he says it is to sacrifice them to the LORD. When Samuel confronts him, Saul first claims he obeyed, then blames the people, then offers religious reasons.

Samuel’s reply is one of the great sentences of the Bible: “Has the LORD as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the LORD? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice.” God is not looking for religious performance but for a surrendered heart. Rebellion is as the sin of divination, and presumption is as iniquity and idolatry.

Saul’s confession is shallow. He says, “I have sinned,” but he immediately asks Samuel to honor him before the elders. He is more worried about his reputation than about his sin. Repentance that seeks to keep the appearance of standing is not true repentance.

The chapter ends with Samuel mourning for Saul, and “the LORD regretted that he had made Saul king.” The word “regret” here speaks of sorrow and a change of course, not of God being surprised. Verse 29 insists that God does not change his mind like a man. His purposes stand.
connection: Jesus quotes Hosea 6:6 twice, “I desire mercy, and not sacrifice” (Matthew 9:13; 12:7), in the same spirit as Samuel. Hebrews 10:5-10 says that Christ came to do God’s will, where sacrifices could not satisfy. Jesus was “obedient to the point of death” (Philippians 2:8), succeeding where Saul failed. John 14:15: “If you love me, you will keep my commandments.”
application:
Ask where you offer God religious activity instead of obedience.

Look at your last confession of sin. Was it about the sin, or about how you look?

Thank Jesus that he obeyed fully, and ask for a listening heart.
prayerPrompts: Confess where you have offered God less than your heart.
Ask for the faith of Jonathan, who believed nothing can hinder God.
Thank Christ for his perfect obedience.
